summary: Mission Memory is an educational detective game about NASA equipment left on the Moon and Mars. Players choose from 11 mission cases, explore a 3D scene, inspect NASA imagery and clue markers, and reconstruct what each machine achieved and why it remains behind. In the Opportunity case, players connect layered rock, sulfate minerals, and hematite-rich spherules to the supported conclusion that liquid water interacted with ancient Martian rock. The game does not claim that Opportunity found life. Each case ends with the machine’s purpose, discovery, and legacy. NASA mission records, images, and selected 3D models ground the stories. Simple View, browser read-aloud, reduced-motion support, and saved progress help school-age learners and casual visitors participate. Mission Memory makes discarded hardware a starting point for understanding how evidence becomes scientific knowledge.
details:
Mission Memory responds to “Abandoned but not Forgotten” by telling the stories of real NASA machines that remained on the Moon or Mars. The browser game offers 11 playable cases: four lunar cases (Apollo 11 Eagle, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP, and Surveyor 3) and seven Martian cases (Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking, Phoenix, InSight, and Ingenuity).

Players choose a case, explore a 3D mission setting, select clue markers or numbered clue buttons, study mission images and observations, answer short questions, and solve a final mystery. Each ending explains what the equipment was built to do, what it achieved, why it stopped or remains behind, and how its work shaped later exploration. Opportunity includes a deeper evidence board and a four-stop, photo-led journey.

The learning goal is to distinguish observations from conclusions. Opportunity’s rock layers, sulfate-related minerals, and hematite-rich spherules together support a history of liquid water interacting with ancient Martian rock; they do not prove that the rover discovered life. NASA mission records, photographs, maps, and selected 3D spacecraft models provide scientific context. The game labels its artistic terrain reconstructions.

Designed for approximately ages 9–14 and casual space enthusiasts, the game supports touch, mouse, and keyboard. Simple View allows cases to be completed without 3D; browser read-aloud and reduced-motion support broaden access. Progress saves locally, and no account or backend is required.

We developed the client with React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, and React Three Fiber. Our creative approach treats left-behind hardware as the beginning of a scientific mystery. We considered scientific accuracy, source attribution, short play sessions, accessibility, browser performance, and the limits of artistic reconstruction. We hope the game helps more people understand how mission evidence becomes knowledge, and why a machine’s contribution continues after it stops operating.
